title: From Legal Aid to LIT Lab: Quinten Steenhuis and the Builder’s Approach to AI
author: Quinten Steenhuis

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Steenhuis accepts that AI disrupts how lawyers acquire foundational skills and materially extends the cluster’s response by proposing simulations, practice sessions and tailored feedback while preserving the ability to verify imperfect AI work. He presents these as promising educational mechanisms, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Quinten Steenhuis (34:33)  In academia, I think our big challenge is going to be how do we help people learn the things that they need to learn when there’s an AI that can do those things for them very quickly, but just not perfectly.
It can help with simulations, practice sessions, giving people instant feedback in a way that one law professor couldn’t possibly keep up with to give really tailored education.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Steenhuis accepts the cluster’s core emphasis on selective, institutionally supported deployment rather than model access alone. He materially develops it by specifying reliable, testable end-to-end use cases, additional verification mechanisms, AI-enabled training, and accessible alternatives for self-represented litigants.
qs: What can we do that’s reliable, testable, end to end?
We can’t just say, hey, just use AI in these safe ways and then don’t give people an alternative.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Steenhuis accepts the need for selective, verified deployment and materially extends the cluster with a builder’s framework: engineer reliable, testable end-to-end use cases, redesign training so users can detect failures, and develop accessible alternatives for people already relying on unsafe general-purpose AI.
qs: What can we do that’s reliable, testable, end to end?
So it’s really hard to figure out how much time we spend on practicing rote skills that the AI can do really well 90 % of the time and help them to be prepared to catch the 10%.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that agentic AI shifts legal technology from text generation toward autonomous task execution, including connected administrative work such as intake, scheduling and eligibility checks. It remains high-level and prospective, however, and does not address differing autonomy levels, error propagation, verification bottlenecks, governance or deployment evidence.
qs: I think agentic AI is like a really interesting term because it sounds really fancy, but as you said, right, it’s really just AI that can do things for us besides just like responding with text.
so where do you see a shift to where we can get these AI agents to begin to autonomously handle, you know,  administrative burdens of legal aid, say like intake or scheduling or eligibility checks.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s claim that legal-AI product coverage continues to expand and is shifting toward operational workflows. It does not, however, provide evidence about adoption, performance, renewal economics or realized value, so its support is limited to the supply-side expansion component.
qs: And it has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.
In December, interestingly, that had cooled a little bit and the hot concentration of startup activity had shifted over into operational tools.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Steenhuis directly accepts the competence paradox: learners must retain enough routine practice to detect AI failures. He also endorses the cluster’s proposed response through simulations, practice and tailored feedback, while acknowledging that training remains difficult.
qs: So it’s really hard to figure out how much time we spend on practicing rote skills that the AI can do really well 90 % of the time and help them to be prepared to catch the 10%.
It can help with simulations, practice sessions, giving people instant feedback in a way that one law professor couldn’t possibly keep up with to give really tailored education.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source directly supports selective, network-based continuous learning rather than indiscriminate news chasing, and reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on preserving verification skills as AI capabilities evolve. Its voice-AI and market observations add context but do not materially alter the cluster’s proposition.
qs: So I try not to procrastinate too much by reading all this news from the fire hose every day, every minute, but I do appreciate it.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s move beyond isolated text generation toward AI that executes legal-service tasks, including prospective legal-aid intake, scheduling and eligibility workflows. It also supports multidisciplinary exchange as an implementation condition, but offers no deployment evidence and does not address pricing, verification or apprenticeship directly.
qs: Is the future of legal tech less about the requesting for a memo to be drafted and more about go do this and finish this task?
I think agentic AI is like a really interesting term because it sounds really fancy, but as you said, right, it’s really just AI that can do things for us besides just like responding with text.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Steenhuis aligns closely with the synthesis: he favors bounded, reliable and testable legal-AI uses, requires additional checks for imperfect outputs, and recognizes that AI-enabled efficiency creates a training problem because users still need enough competence to detect failures. His warning about self-represented litigants also supports the distinction between access to AI tools and effective access to justice.
qs: What can we do that’s reliable, testable, end to end?
So it’s really hard to figure out how much time we spend on practicing rote skills that the AI can do really well 90 % of the time and help them to be prepared to catch the 10%.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that useful legal AI requires guided human participation rather than unguided use. It recommends harm reduction and safer assistance for ChatGPT users, while offering no specific safeguards or empirical evidence of effectiveness.
qs: And how do we kind of do a harm reduction against the alternative, which is really just people going wild with ChatGPT and doing whatever they want.
So we need to figure it out, helping people do it safely.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Steenhuis supports selective, bounded AI augmentation by prioritising reliable, testable use cases and additional safeguards for imperfect outputs. He also reinforces the cluster’s junior-development and access-to-justice tensions: AI may enable personalised training, but safe-use guidance is inadequate without practical alternatives for self-represented litigants.
qs: What can we do that’s reliable, testable, end to end?
We need to add something as an extra check to help solve that.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on multidisciplinary collaboration and concrete workflow problems, endorsing community exchange and task-performing AI for functions such as intake, scheduling and eligibility checks. Its support is prospective and conceptual, however; it provides no implementation results, connected-data strategy or account of organisational incentives and resources.
qs: And I think it’s really critical to kind of have that kind of ability to talk to each other about what we’re doing.
so where do you see a shift to where we can get these AI agents to begin to autonomously handle, you know,  administrative burdens of legal aid, say like intake or scheduling or eligibility checks.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Steenhuis supports the cluster’s bounded, task-sensitive account: AI can perform routine work and aid learning, but imperfect outputs require additional checks, deliberate training and reliable end-to-end use cases. His account of self-represented litigants also reinforces the cluster’s warning that cheaper assistance can shift burdens to courts unless practical alternatives and safeguards exist. He does not make a staffing or aggregate employment claim.
qs: We need to add something as an extra check to help solve that.
We can’t just say, hey, just use AI in these safe ways and then don’t give people an alternative.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Shaver directly supports the cluster’s account of an expanding legal-AI vendor landscape and a reported shift in startup activity toward operational tools. Her figures describe map coverage and her explanation of category crowding remains tentative, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary cautions.
qs: And it has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.

kp.k: Legal AI vendor mapping shows continued growth and shifting activity
kp.d: Nikki Shaver reports that Legal Technology Hub’s map, with a cutoff at the end of December 2025, contains 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, with about 100 companies added each quarter. She reports that December startup activity shifted from broad AI legal assistants toward operational tools for firms and legal departments, including intake, compliance and governance. She interprets the assistant category as potentially settled and crowded, and the mapping trajectory as showing no slowdown; these are her interpretations of the mapping, not independent evidence of market sustainability.
qs: The cutoff date for that was the end of December 2025. And it has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.
The growth trajectory has been incredibly consistent and steady with about 100 companies added to the map every quarter.
In December, interestingly, that had cooled a little bit and the hot concentration of startup activity had shifted over into operational tools.
it also suggests that maybe new entrants are seeing the broad assistant category as being relatively settled right now and also quite crowded.

kp.k: Foundational AI instruction leads into sustained practical legal training
kp.d: Asked about Suffolk’s required first-year generative AI learning track, Steenhuis describes foundational instruction followed by electives and practical application throughout law school. His small-firm legal technology seminar has progressively incorporated generative AI since 2023, now devoting about half its time to it, while the lab provides 12 students with a full-year clinical building experience. He acknowledges that introductory instruction may feel like a checkbox exercise for some students, but presents its value as preparation for continued use and learning.
qs: We’re learning the basics, we’re giving everyone a foundation to build on.
So for some folks, it might be a little bit of a checkbox exercise to learn just those foundational skills.
And now it’s about half of the thing that we spend our times on.
And then in our lab, we take students and give them a full year clinical experience, 12 students that are learning and building with these same tools.

kp.k: Standardised infrastructure and supervision sustain student-built legal tools
kp.d: Steenhuis attributes the lab’s ability to maintain tools beyond student projects to concentrating on a small set of supportable technologies, notably DocAssemble, alongside clinician supervision, court partnerships and regular review. Students complete a small semester-launch project and a larger paired project by year-end. Tools are published on courtformsonline.org, with staff and volunteer maintenance. Indefinite support is an institutional commitment he describes, while another 10, 20 or 30 years of technical longevity remains his expectation.
qs: we decided to streamline our focus and to really zero in on a couple of core technologies that we really felt, yeah, we can support this.
These tools get regular updates and review.
We have volunteers who help with some of those steps and we take that on ourselves and just guarantee once we launch it, we’re committed to keeping it going indefinitely.
I think we can probably stay around for another 10 years with these tools, maybe 20 or 30.

kp.k: Open-source document automation supports direct public legal assistance
kp.d: As background to current AI development, Steenhuis describes using DocAssemble to build Made, an eviction-defense paperwork tool serving lawyers, non-attorney advocates and tenants directly. He identifies free, flexible open-source infrastructure as supporting both legal-aid tools and commercial software products. This is an account of document automation infrastructure rather than a claim that these earlier tools used generative AI.
qs: So I built a tool called Made that was, in a way, TurboTax for eviction defense, helping attorneys maybe with a client or
other kinds of non-attorney advocates, as well as tenants directly to help fill in all of the eviction defense paperwork that they needed to do accurately, correctly.
So anybody can run it for free. There’ve been several commercial software products built on top of it because it’s available for free.

kp.k: Legal-aid technology requires implementation capacity, not merely cheap software
kp.d: Steenhuis recounts that corporate philanthropy gave a low-resourced legal-aid organisation access to enterprise tools from providers including Microsoft, Twilio and Amazon. He stresses experimentation and assessing whether tools could scale appropriately to the organisation’s needs. This historical implementation experience qualifies the builder approach: low acquisition costs do not remove the need to choose technologies that staff can support.
qs: We were low resourced, but we’d access to these really big enterprise level tools for free or very low cost.
I can experiment with this and figure out is this too big for our needs or is it something we can scale?
we had to be careful for sure to know that they weren’t too big for our size of organization.

kp.k: Clinical technology education cultivates curiosity and independent problem-solving
kp.d: Steenhuis reports that some students entering with the least technical self-identification became the clinic’s best performers. With no prerequisites, students learn software building under supervision. He emphasises curiosity, perseverance and identifying the steps toward a goal rather than waiting for instructions, describing this capacity as potentially the most transferable skill the clinic provides. These are observations from his teaching, not measured comparative educational outcomes.
qs: I’ve seen some of our folks who entered as the least technical, least self-identified as being technical be our best performers in the clinic.
they don’t have any prereqs, so they can join and they learn from the beginning start to finish how to build software tools with our support.
I can’t just wait for someone to tell me the next step. I have to learn it and figure it out.
That might be the most transferable skill that we can give our students is helping them do that growth.

kp.k: Practitioner-academic collaboration connects AI safety with real-world usability
kp.d: Steenhuis describes recurring AI and access-to-justice workshops, most recently their fifth edition in Turin, as a mechanism for joining practitioner needs with academic research. Practitioners seek evidence that tools work and methods for ensuring safety and quality, while academics seek relevance, usability and deployment. He presents this exchange, supported by Suffolk’s leadership, as a way to bridge the two communities rather than treating research or rapid building as sufficient alone.
qs: We’ve been doing these regular AI and access to justice workshops.
What are the ways I ensure the quality and safety of this? How do I understand, does this thing work? People launch things without necessarily knowing that all the time.
How do I actually know if this thing is usable? Do people actually know which buttons to click?
Both of those sides are really interested in hearing from each other.

kp.k: Voice AI automates legal-aid intake screening before attorney contact
kp.d: Steenhuis reports building a voice-based intake system for Virginia Legal Aid Society through his consulting work. It checks service location and income, elicits the caller’s legal problem in their own words, asks follow-up questions and uses a classification tool to match the problem against possible categories. He presents this as action-oriented AI beyond text generation, with attorney contact following screening. He also stresses sensitively handling requests that cannot be addressed by a lawyer; no screening accuracy or service-outcome measurements are supplied.
qs: we’ve built a AI voice-based intake system.
And it goes from start to finish of the screening steps of helping somebody get matched with an attorney.
It confirms things like their income. And it also gets them to use their own words to describe their legal problem.
And then it uses a tool that we built to help classify that person’s legal problem from a long list of possible categories.
We have to handle those really sensitively, but we want to help screen those people out as well.

kp.k: Automated bar referrals replace delayed attorney review
kp.d: For the Oregon State Bar’s referral service, Steenhuis describes using the same legal-problem matching technology without voice, which he judged inappropriate for that project. He says it provides an instant referral instead of the previous process in which an attorney reviewed a web submission and supplied a referral a day or two later. This is a reported operational change in referral work, not evidence of equivalent referral quality or wider lawyer displacement.
qs: We’re helping with their bar referral service. And it’s using that same technology, that legal problem matching technology.
We’re not using voice for that project. It didn’t really seem like the appropriate technology to use, but it gives them an instant referral.
Whereas what would happen before is that someone would put something in in a web form, attorney would look it over, and then take a day or two to give them a referral.

kp.k: AI interfaces can reduce reliance on open-ended chat
kp.d: Steenhuis advocates interfaces that convert users’ descriptions into generated forms, selectable alternatives and yes-or-no questions rather than requiring extensive typing. He reports experimenting with these approaches and says they are already being used, while anticipating further interaction models. His stated aim is a more efficient, pleasant experience, particularly on phones; he supplies no comparative usability results.
qs: With these new tools, we could give people a form to interact with instead. And it can be generated by AI.
Ask some yes or no questions that again, the person could just click rather than having to type out an answer.
And so we’re really playing around with these ideas to improve the user experience of interacting with AI
I can just see new metaphors and ways of interacting with AI that help make it a better experience for everybody coming in the future.

kp.k: Modular voice infrastructure could help bridge digital access gaps
kp.d: Steenhuis identifies the open-source Pipecat platform as the basis for a modular speech-to-text, AI and text-to-speech workflow that allows experimentation with new models. Separately, he reports hearing about a voice-powered AI project for people in Niger with small language populations, low literacy and little technological access beyond a phone. He sees voice interaction as a promising access-enabling technology; this is a reported project and prospective benefit, not demonstrated access-to-justice impact.
qs: And there’s a tool called Pipecat.
So we, as new AI models are released, we can experiment with embedding those into the tool.
And it uses this loop from speech to text. We have the AI do its piece. Then there’s text to speech.
one of the other projects that was discussed was a voice powered AI agent for folks in Niger.
Really the most advanced technology they have is a phone.

kp.k: AI creates a training challenge around human verification
kp.d: Looking ahead, Steenhuis identifies a dilemma for legal education: students must learn to check work that AI can produce quickly but imperfectly, requiring decisions about how much practice in underlying skills to retain. His 90%/10% language illustrates this dilemma rather than reporting a model evaluation. He predicts that simulations, practice sessions and instant tailored feedback could help address it, while acknowledging the continuing challenge.
qs: how do we help people learn the things that they need to learn when there’s an AI that can do those things for them very quickly, but just not perfectly. And they need to check the work.
it’s really hard to figure out how much time we spend on practicing rote skills that the AI can do really well 90 % of the time and help them to be prepared to catch the 10%.
It can help with simulations, practice sessions, giving people instant feedback in a way that one law professor couldn’t possibly keep up with to give really tailored education.

kp.k: Safe AI requires engineering checks and public-facing alternatives
kp.d: Steenhuis argues that hallucinations and other quality problems require additional checks and engineering, favouring reliable, testable end-to-end use cases. He also warns that self-represented litigants already ask ChatGPT to draft motions and claims, sometimes producing nonsense documents that courts must address. He frames the response as harm reduction: recommending safe uses alone is inadequate without alternatives for the public. The transcript supplies no incident counts or measured error rates for this claim.
qs: We need to add something as an extra check to help solve that. Other quality issues too, not just hallucinations.
For me, I focus on safe use cases. What can we do that’s reliable, testable, end to end?
self-represented litigants are just going to ChatGPT and saying, write me a motion or help me file this claim.
And generating sometimes nonsense documents that the court has to respond to.
We can’t just say, hey, just use AI in these safe ways and then don’t give people an alternative.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nikki Shaver reports continued expansion of the generative-AI legal-tech market and says her earlier forecast of 1,000 product placements remains on track.
pts.d: In the opening market update, Shaver attributes this assessment to Legal Technology Hub's successive maps. The latest map, released in early January with a December 2025 cutoff, contains 855 product placements from 682 vendors across 19 categories. She reports approximately 100 companies added per quarter and interprets this as no slowdown yet. Her 1,000-product forecast was made in March of the preceding year for a year later, implying approximately March 2026. These are mapped vendor and product counts, not evidence of revenue growth, profitability or customer adoption.

pts.k: Shaver reports a shift in startup activity from broad AI legal assistants toward operational, compliance and governance tools.
pts.d: She contrasts December 2025 with most of the preceding year, when AI Legal Assistant was the hottest category. The newer concentration includes work and client intake for law firms and corporate legal departments. Her evidence is comparison of successive maps, alongside her market observations. She presents the explanation that entrants regard broad assistants as crowded and relatively settled as a possibility, not an established finding.

pts.k: Quinten Steenhuis says AI can execute legal-aid intake screening rather than merely generate text.
pts.d: Drawing on his consulting work, Steenhuis describes a voice-based system built for Virginia Legal Aid Society that handles screening from start to finish: location, income, a caller's account of the problem, follow-up questions and classification against legal-problem categories. This is a report of a built application, not a forecast of replacing attorneys. The workflow screens for service fit and leads to an attorney conversation. He notes the need for sensitive treatment of people whose problems are not amenable to legal assistance. No accuracy, completion-rate or staffing-savings measurements are supplied.

pts.k: Steenhuis reports that AI-based legal-problem matching makes bar referrals immediate and argues that structured interfaces can make AI easier to use than open-ended chat.
pts.d: For the Oregon State Bar referral service, he describes using the same matching technology through a non-voice interface. He contrasts instant referrals with the prior process of attorney review followed by a referral one or two days later. This substitutes for an intermediate review step in that referral workflow, not for substantive representation. More broadly, he describes experimenting with AI-generated forms, selectable choices and yes/no questions to reduce typing, especially on phones. The referral timing is a practitioner-reported before-and-after comparison; improved interface efficiency and pleasantness are asserted without user-study results. He says such tools are already in use and anticipates additional interaction approaches.

pts.k: Steenhuis sees voice AI as a way to bridge digital-access barriers for people with limited literacy or only basic telephone access.
pts.d: His assessment combines experience building with the modular, open-source Pipecat platform and exposure to a voice-agent project for people in Niger at a recent workshop. He describes separating speech recognition, AI processing and speech synthesis so components can be selected or updated independently. The access claim concerns people without smartphones or internet access, including small-language populations. It is an enabling-technology argument, not a demonstrated improvement in legal outcomes or a claim that language coverage and accessibility have been fully solved.

pts.k: Steenhuis predicts that AI will require legal education to balance foundational practice with verification skills, while enabling more individualized practice and feedback.
pts.d: He describes Suffolk's current approach as foundational first-year exposure followed by electives and hands-on clinical work across the degree. He reports increasing generative-AI content in his small-firm technology seminar since 2023, now occupying approximately half the course. Looking ahead, he identifies a teaching problem: students must learn enough to catch errors even when AI performs routine tasks quickly. He anticipates simulations, practice sessions and instant feedback that a single professor could not supply at comparable scale. His 90%/10% language illustrates this dilemma; the transcript provides no benchmark or measured student-performance evidence for those percentages.

pts.k: Steenhuis expects additional checks and engineering to improve AI reliability, but argues that safe alternatives are also needed for self-represented litigants already using general-purpose AI.
pts.d: In the near-future discussion, Steenhuis predicts increased attention to hallucinations and other quality problems. He characterizes hallucinations as core to how large language models work and advocates additional checks and reliable, end-to-end testable use cases. Separately, he says self-represented litigants already ask ChatGPT to draft motions or help file claims, sometimes producing nonsense documents that courts must address. He argues that merely recommending narrow safe uses is inadequate without alternatives, framing the task as harm reduction. These are practitioner assessments and predictions; no named court incidents, error-rate studies or validated mitigation results are provided. He does not claim that engineering will eliminate every error.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines descriptive market counts with firsthand implementation and teaching experience; its broader forecasts are not supported by formal performance studies in the transcript.
pts.d: Shaver supplies dated product-placement and vendor counts from Legal Technology Hub maps. Steenhuis supplies named implementation examples at Virginia Legal Aid Society and the Oregon State Bar, a reported referral-time comparison, and details of Suffolk teaching practice. He mentions a conference award for the work presented, but an award is not an accuracy or safety evaluation. The Niger example comes from a workshop presentation rather than his own deployment. Predictions about educational personalization, interface improvement and reliability engineering are reasoned expectations. No benchmark, controlled evaluation, measured hallucination rate or quantified access-to-justice outcome is reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Market observations are dated to the end of 2025; operational applications are described as current, while educational and reliability changes have an unspecified near-future horizon.
pts.d: The opening update uses a December 2025 map cutoff and reports a shift during that December. The earlier 1,000-product forecast points to roughly March 2026. Steenhuis describes intake and referral tools as already built or being used, and expanding seminar content since 2023. He offers no calendar deadline for new educational strategies, interfaces or quality-control advances. Conditions include selecting an appropriate interface rather than assuming voice is always suitable, maintaining human error-checking competence, and using reliable, testable workflows. Current operational automation should not be read as a forecast of autonomous legal representation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern legal-tech vendors and buyers, legal-aid applicants and referral staff, underserved communities, law students and educators, and courts dealing with AI-assisted self-representation.
pts.d: Vendors face a growing and potentially crowded assistant market, while firms and corporate legal departments are targets for operational tools. Legal-aid applicants can describe problems in their own words and undergo automated screening before speaking with an attorney; bar-referral users receive faster matching, with less intermediate attorney review. People with low literacy or limited digital access may benefit from telephone-based interfaces. Law students need both practical AI fluency and the ability to verify imperfect outputs; educators face curriculum redesign and potential gains from tailored feedback. Self-represented litigants face risks from unsuitable AI-generated filings, and courts bear the burden of responding. The source does not quantify job displacement, firm staffing changes, legal-fee reductions or improved case outcomes.
